title: False Teachers and Certain Judgment
summary: Peter exposes false teachers who deny their Redeemer, assures the faithful that God rescues the godly, and warns of apostasy’s ruin.
historicalContext: Peter writes near the end of his life (1:14) to believers who had received the apostolic gospel and were now being courted by teachers from within their own fellowship. These teachers ate at the church’s common meals, used Christian vocabulary, and promised a freedom that loosened moral restraint. Their appeal fitted the surrounding culture, where sexual license was common, rhetoric was a marketable skill, and popular philosophy taught that the gods do not intervene in human affairs. Combined with the apparent delay of Christ’s return, that outlook allowed them to dismiss future judgment as an empty threat (3:3–4). Peter answers from Israel’s Scriptures. The fallen angels, the flood, Sodom, and Balaam were familiar stories, and Jude’s short letter, which shares much of this material, shows that other congregations faced the same danger.
literaryContext: Chapter 2 turns sharply from the true prophecy of 1:19–21 to its counterfeit, and it prepares for the scoffers of chapter 3. The first paragraph (2:1–3) names the teachers, their method, and their doom. A single long sentence (2:4–10a) then sets out three precedents of judgment, two of them paired with rescue, and draws the conclusion that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly and keep the unjust for the day of judgment. The rest of the chapter is a vivid portrait built from animal images, Balaam’s story, natural metaphors, and proverbs. Throughout, the language of “the way” (2:2, 15, 21) sets the path of truth against the wandering road of error, and the chapter’s vices stand in deliberate contrast to the virtues of 1:5–7.
themes: Counterfeit teaching that denies the Master who bought it
The certainty of judgment despite apparent delay
God’s ability to rescue the godly
Greed and sensuality as marks of false religion
Freedom promised by those enslaved to corruption
The grave danger of turning back from known truth

outline.title: False Teachers Among You
outline.summary: As Israel had false prophets, the church will face teachers who smuggle in ruinous error, deny their Redeemer, exploit believers, and meet a judgment that is not asleep.

outline.title: Precedents of Judgment and Rescue
outline.summary: The fallen angels, the flood, and Sodom show that God judges the ungodly, while Noah and Lot show that he knows how to deliver the godly.

outline.title: A Portrait of Arrogance and Appetite
outline.summary: The teachers despise authority, revile what they do not understand, carouse at the church’s meals, and follow Balaam’s greedy road.

outline.title: Empty Promises and the Way Back to the Mire
outline.summary: Their promises of freedom are dry springs; those who return to the world after knowing Christ end in a worse state than before.

verses.bibleText: But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The opening “But” turns sharply from the close of chapter 1. Peter has just described true prophecy as speech that came when holy men were carried along by the Holy Spirit. Israel’s history had another side. Alongside the true prophets stood counterfeit ones who claimed the Lord’s name for messages of their own making (Deuteronomy 13; Jeremiah 23). Peter expects the pattern to repeat. “There shall be” looks ahead, yet later in the chapter he shifts into present and past tenses, which suggests the danger is already active somewhere and moving closer. He also changes the title from prophets to teachers. These people may not claim new revelation at all; they reinterpret the message the church has already received.

“Privily shall bring in” pictures something carried in alongside, as contraband travels with ordinary cargo. “Damnable heresies” is literally “heresies of destruction.” The word hairesis could once describe a school of thought or a chosen opinion, but here it names teaching that splits the fellowship and whose end is ruin. The rest of the letter fills in its content: contempt for the Lord’s authority, permission for sensuality, and the claim that Christ will not return in judgment (3:3–4).

The most startling charge is “denying the Lord that bought them.” The title is despotēs, the master who owns a household of slaves, and “bought” recalls the price paid to acquire them. The price was Christ’s own blood (1 Peter 1:18–19). Two truths stand side by side. Christ’s purchase reached even those who would finally reject it, and their denial was real because they had once confessed him. Peter knew the weight of that word from a courtyard fire, and he also knew how quickly his Lord restored a repentant denier. What marks these teachers is persistence without repentance.

They bring “upon themselves swift destruction.” The adjective translated “swift” describes Peter’s own approaching death in 1:14, so it stresses nearness and certainty more than speed. The destruction (apōleia) is the final loss that the New Testament sets opposite salvation (Philippians 1:28). His judgment confirms the end of the road they have chosen.

wordNotes.term: τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτοὺς δεσπότην (ton agorasanta autous despotēn) — the Lord that bought them
wordNotes.explanation: Despotēs is the owner of slaves, a title stressing full authority, and the participle refers to acquiring them by purchase. Early Christians used this commercial language for redemption through Christ’s death. To deny such a Master is both rebellion and ingratitude, because he has paid the price for the very people who disown him.

wordNotes.term: αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας (haireseis apōleias) — damnable heresies
wordNotes.explanation: Hairesis can describe a party or a chosen opinion. Joined to apōleia, “destruction,” it describes teachings that divide the community and lead their followers to ruin. Peter uses apōleia repeatedly in this letter for the final destruction of the ungodly.

verses.bibleText: And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter does not pretend the danger will be small. “Many shall follow” uses a verb he applied in 1:16 to following clever myths, and he will use it again for those who follow Balaam’s way (2:15). It is the language of discipleship turned inside out. People will attach themselves to these teachers and imitate them.

What they follow is described as “pernicious ways.” The better-attested reading is aselgeiais, acts of unrestrained indulgence, and the same word reappears in verses 7 and 18. Peter assumes that belief and behavior travel together. A message that loosens moral restraint attracts followers because it flatters the desires people already have. Popularity proves nothing about truth. A crowd can be large precisely because the road is easy (Matthew 7:13).

The second consequence reaches beyond the church: “the way of truth shall be evil spoken of.” The wording recalls Isaiah 52:5, where Israel’s unfaithfulness caused God’s name to be reviled among the nations. Outsiders do not separate faithful believers from those who merely carry the Christian name. When people associated with the church behave shamefully, the gospel itself is blamed. Peter’s first letter urged believers to live so honestly among unbelievers that slander would collapse (1 Peter 2:12). Here he describes the reverse.

Calling the faith “the way of truth” is telling. Christianity is a road to be walked as well as a message to be believed (Acts 9:2). Its truth is meant to become visible in conduct, which is why corrupted conduct discredits it so quickly.

wordNotes.term: ταῖς ἀσελγείαις (tais aselgeiais) — pernicious ways
wordNotes.explanation: The strongest manuscript evidence supports aselgeiais, “licentious acts,” rather than the reading behind the KJV. The word describes behavior without restraint, often sexual. The plural points to specific deeds, not merely an attitude.

wordNotes.term: ἡ ὁδὸς τῆς ἀληθείας (hē hodos tēs alētheias) — the way of truth
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes the Christian faith as a path of life shaped by truth. It anticipates “the right way” (2:15) and “the way of righteousness” (2:21), and stands in contrast to the wandering road of error.

verses.bibleText: And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now exposes the motive and the method. The motive is “covetousness,” pleonexia, the craving for more that is willing to take from others to get it. The New Testament often places this vice beside sexual sin (Ephesians 5:3), and the two appear together throughout this chapter. These teachers are not disinterested seekers of truth. Their message pays.

The method is “feigned words.” The adjective plastos means molded or shaped, and from it comes the English word plastic. Their speech is fashioned to fit the audience, adjusted for effect rather than faithful to reality. With such words they “make merchandise of you.” The verb comes from the world of trade, and the shocking point is that the believers themselves become the goods. Ministry has turned into commerce, and souls into profit. Paul repeatedly distanced himself from teachers who peddled the word for gain (2 Corinthians 2:17; 1 Thessalonians 2:5), and the contrast with Balaam later in the chapter is already in view.

Then comes a double assurance about judgment. “Whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not” speaks of a verdict (krima) long since determined that has not gone idle. “Their damnation slumbereth not” pictures destruction as a watchman who never nods off at his post. Peter seems to anticipate the scoffers’ argument of 3:4: because nothing has happened for a long time, nothing will happen. His reply is that delay does not mean inactivity. The God of Israel “neither slumbers nor sleeps” (Psalm 121:4), and his sentence is as wakeful as he is. The reason for the delay will be given in 3:9: his patience is holding the door open for repentance.

The verse supplies a practical test. Teaching that serves its hearers builds them up in Christ, while teaching that uses them treats them as a market. The apparent success of the second kind says nothing about its final outcome.

wordNotes.term: πλαστοῖς λόγοις ἐμπορεύσονται (plastois logois emporeusontai) — with feigned words make merchandise
wordNotes.explanation: Plastos describes something fabricated or molded to a purpose; emporeuomai means to trade or do business. Together they picture teachers who shape persuasive speech in order to profit from their hearers, treating believers as merchandise.

wordNotes.term: οὐ νυστάζει (ou nystazei) — slumbereth not
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to nod or doze, as the waiting virgins did in Jesus’ parable. Peter personifies destruction as alert and on its way. Whatever delay there seems to be, judgment has not dozed off.

verses.bibleText: For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verses 4–10a form one long conditional sentence. “For if God” introduces three precedents, arranged in historical order, and the conclusion arrives only in verse 9: “The Lord knoweth how.” Peter is answering teachers who say God does not step into history to judge. The record shows that he has, and that he has also preserved the righteous when he did.

The first precedent is “the angels that sinned.” Peter does not describe their sin; he assumes his readers know the story. Elsewhere Scripture speaks of rebellion in heaven, of the dragon and his angels cast out to the earth (Revelation 12:7–9), and of Satan falling like lightning (Luke 10:18). Some Jewish writings connected the angelic fall with Genesis 6, but Peter’s argument does not rest on that interpretation. His point is simpler and sharper. Beings who had stood in God’s presence were not spared when they rebelled. If such privilege did not shelter them, religious standing will not shelter teachers who deny their Master.

“Cast them down to hell” translates a single Greek verb, tartaroō, formed from Tartarus, the deepest pit of Greek mythology where rebel Titans were confined. Peter borrows a word his Hellenistic readers would recognize in order to convey confinement under sentence. He does not thereby endorse the mythology. “Chains of darkness” (or, in many manuscripts, “pits of darkness”) is likewise figurative. The fallen angels are still active, for the devil prowls as a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), so the picture describes restriction and a doomed condition, cut off from the light of God, rather than a literal dungeon.

The decisive words are “to be reserved unto judgment.” The present participle describes custody that continues while the verdict waits to be carried out. The final punishment of the devil and his angels lies at the end, in the fire prepared for them (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). Peter does not describe angels, or human beings, already undergoing their final punishment in an ongoing hell. He describes rebels held for a day of judgment that is certain. The same verb of keeping will be used of the unjust in verse 9 and of the present heavens and earth in 3:7.

wordNotes.term: ταρταρώσας (tartarōsas) — cast them down to hell
wordNotes.explanation: This verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to consign to Tartarus. Peter uses a term familiar to his Greek-speaking readers to express confinement under sentence, without adopting the pagan picture of the underworld. The context defines the condition: the angels are kept for judgment, not yet given their final punishment.

wordNotes.term: εἰς κρίσιν τηρουμένους (eis krisin tēroumenous) — to be reserved unto judgment
wordNotes.explanation: Tēreō means to keep or guard, often of prisoners held in custody. The present participle stresses continuing detention, and krisis points to the act of judgment still to come. Peter uses the same verb for the unjust (2:9) and for the present world (3:7).

verses.bibleText: And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second precedent is “the old world,” the human society that existed before the flood. Genesis describes it as a world whose every imagination was only evil continually and whose earth was filled with violence (Genesis 6:5, 11). God “spared not” this world, using the same verb as in verse 4.

Yet in the middle of the judgment stands a rescue. God “saved Noah,” and the verb (phylassō) means to guard or keep safe. The keeping of verse 4 holds the rebels for judgment; the keeping of verse 5 shelters Noah through it. One sovereign care produces opposite outcomes depending on the response of those it touches. “Noah the eighth person” is an idiom meaning Noah with seven others, his wife, his sons, and their wives (Genesis 7:7; 1 Peter 3:20). On the day the rain began, the majority was wrong.

Noah is called “a preacher of righteousness.” The word kērux names a herald who announces a message on behalf of a ruler. Genesis records no sermons, but Noah’s years of building the ark were a public proclamation in themselves, condemning the world by his faith (Hebrews 11:7). Peter’s first letter shows who was speaking through that witness: Christ, by the Spirit, appealed to that generation through Noah while God’s patience waited (1 Peter 3:18–20). The righteousness Noah heralded was the right relationship with God and the upright life it produces, the same righteousness that will fill the new earth (3:13).

God brought “in the flood upon the world of the ungodly.” The verb is the one used in verse 1 for the teachers bringing destruction on themselves. Jesus used the days of Noah to describe the suddenness of his own return (Matthew 24:37–39), and Peter will return to the flood in 3:5–7 as a preview of the final judgment. Long warning, ignored by most, followed by a decisive end: that is the pattern the scoffers have forgotten.

wordNotes.term: δικαιοσύνης κήρυκα (dikaiosynēs kēryka) — a preacher of righteousness
wordNotes.explanation: A kērux was an official herald who announced a ruler’s message publicly. Noah is presented as God’s herald to a corrupt generation, proclaiming the righteousness God requires and offering a way of escape through his warning and his obedience in building the ark.

wordNotes.term: ἐφύλαξεν (ephylaxen) — saved
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to guard, protect, or keep safe. It recalls the Lord shutting Noah into the ark and stresses that Noah’s preservation was God’s act of protection in the midst of judgment.

verses.bibleText: And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third precedent is Sodom and Gomorrha. Peter fixes attention on the result of their judgment rather than on the fire and brimstone that fell. God turned the cities “into ashes.” The verb tephroō means to reduce to ash, and it was used in Greek writing for towns buried under volcanic ash. Nothing remained to be rebuilt. He “condemned them with an overthrow,” and the noun katastrophē is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Sodom’s destruction (Genesis 19:29). The divine verdict was carried out as total ruin.

The cities were made “an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly.” A hypodeigma is a pattern or specimen, a sample of what something is like. Sodom’s ashes are a preview of the end that awaits ungodliness when it persists. Jude says the cities suffer “the vengeance of eternal fire” (Jude 1:7), and the two descriptions belong together. The fire was eternal in its effect: Sodom never rose again, and no flames burn today on the shores of the Dead Sea. Peter’s language of ashes fits the prophetic picture of the last day, when the wicked are consumed like stubble and become ashes under the feet of the righteous (Malachi 4:1–3). The fire of final judgment ends sin and sinners; it does not preserve them in endless burning.

Peter does not list Sodom’s sins here, though verse 7 mentions their unrestrained conduct. Genesis 19 records an attempted assault on Lot’s guests, and Ezekiel adds pride, excess, careless ease, and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). Sodom’s corruption was sexual, social, and spiritual together, which is why it serves so well as a mirror for teachers who combine sensuality with greed.

The example also carries mercy. Abraham pleaded for the city, and the Lord agreed to spare it for the sake of ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). Jesus used the same story to warn his hearers to be ready for his coming (Luke 17:28–30). The ashes speak because God wants them to be heeded before the final fire falls.

wordNotes.term: τεφρώσας (tephrōsas) — turning into ashes
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to burn to ashes or bury in ash. It stresses the completeness of the destruction: the cities were consumed and left as a permanent ruin. The picture is of an ended existence, not an ongoing fire.

wordNotes.term: ὑπόδειγμα (hypodeigma) — ensample
wordNotes.explanation: A hypodeigma is a model or specimen that shows what something is like. Positively it can be an example to follow; here it is a warning sample of the judgment awaiting persistent ungodliness.

verses.bibleText: And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
As Noah stood beside the flood, Lot stands beside the fire. God “delivered just Lot,” and the verb (rhyomai) is the one Jesus taught his disciples to use in prayer: “deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13). Peter’s interest in judgment never crowds out his interest in rescue.

Calling Lot “just” may surprise a reader of Genesis. Lot chose the well-watered plain with little thought for its moral climate (Genesis 13:10–13), offered his daughters to a violent mob, lingered when told to flee, and ended his story in disgrace. Righteousness in Scripture has never meant a spotless record. Lot believed the warning when his sons-in-law laughed at it, sheltered the messengers, and was troubled by the evil around him. Abraham’s intercession assumed that righteous people might be found in the city (Genesis 18:23–25), and the angels led Lot out by the hand, “the LORD being merciful unto him” (Genesis 19:16). His deliverance was mercy from first to last.

Lot was “vexed,” kataponeō, worn down or oppressed. The word may include the threatened violence at his door (Genesis 19:9) as well as the strain of living among people who mocked God’s order. Their “filthy conversation” means their manner of life, their conduct “in licentiousness.” Peter calls them athesmoi, people who set aside every divine ordinance. The description fits the teachers of verse 2 closely, and that is Peter’s intention. Believers surrounded by the same spirit can take heart from the God who knew how to bring Lot out.

wordNotes.term: ἐρρύσατο (errysato) — delivered
wordNotes.explanation: Rhyomai means to rescue or snatch someone from danger. It is regularly used of God’s saving intervention and links Lot’s escape to the promise of verse 9 that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly.

wordNotes.term: τῶν ἀθέσμων (tōn athesmōn) — the wicked
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes people who live without regard for law or divine ordinance, the lawless. Peter uses it again in 3:17 for the error of the wicked, linking Sodom’s spirit to the false teachers.

verses.bibleText: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The parenthesis explains what Lot’s distress was like. He was “dwelling among them,” a strengthened verb that stresses settled residence in their very midst. He had once pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12); now he lived inside it. Evil reached him “in seeing and hearing,” through every daily sight and sound, and it did so “from day to day.” There was no relief.

He “vexed his righteous soul” with their lawless deeds. The verb basanizō means to torment or torture, and the tense pictures a strain that went on and on. “Soul” here describes Lot himself, his inner life of conscience and feeling. Peter is not speaking of a separate part that survives apart from the body. Lot’s anguish shows that his conscience was still alive. He had not grown numb.

That is the encouragement and the warning of the verse. Grief over sin is a mark of the righteous, as in Ezekiel’s vision, where the faithful are marked because they sigh and cry over the abominations in the city (Ezekiel 9:4). Yet grief that never leads to separation can slowly give way to compromise. Lot’s family absorbed more of Sodom than he did, and his wife looked back. Believers who live among corrupting influences need both a tender conscience and the willingness to step away when God calls.

wordNotes.term: ἐβασάνιζεν (ebasanizen) — vexed
wordNotes.explanation: Basanizō means to torment or put under severe strain. It can describe a boat battered by waves or a person in pain. The imperfect tense presents Lot’s distress as continuous, day after day.

wordNotes.term: ἐγκατοικῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς (enkatoikōn en autois) — dwelling among them
wordNotes.explanation: This rare compound emphasizes residence in the very midst of others. Lot was not visiting Sodom or observing it from a distance; he had made his home there, and the exposure was constant.

verses.bibleText: The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here the long sentence reaches its conclusion. “The Lord knoweth how” uses a verb of knowing with an infinitive, which means to know how to do something and to be able to do it. The precedents have shown two sides of a single competence. God rescued Noah and Lot, and he judged the angels, the flood generation, and Sodom. He can do both at once, and he is not confused about which is which.

First, he knows how “to deliver the godly out of temptations.” Peirasmos covers both trials that press on faith and enticements that pull toward sin, and Noah and Lot faced both. The godly (eusebeis) are those marked by the godliness Peter commended in 1:3 and 1:6. The rescue is “out of” the trial. Noah went through the flood in the ark, and Lot was led out of Sodom while the fire was falling. Believers who pray “lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” may expect the same faithful care, with a way of escape that makes endurance possible (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Second, he knows how “to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished.” The verb is the keeping of verse 4. The participle translated “to be punished” is present in form, and it has been read in two ways. It may express purpose: the unjust are kept so that they will be punished at the judgment. Or it may describe the consequences sin already brings in this life while the final sentence waits. Neither reading places the dead in a realm of present punishment before the judgment. Scripture describes the dead as asleep in the grave until the voice of Christ calls them out (John 5:28–29; Daniel 12:2), and it locates reward and punishment at his coming (Matthew 16:27; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). Peter will identify “the day of judgment” with the day of the Lord in 3:7 and 3:10.

The verse answers both audiences. To the teachers who deny judgment, it says the day is fixed and they are being held for it. To the faithful who feel outnumbered, it says the Lord who brought Noah and Lot through is watching over them. The waiting itself is his patience (3:9).

wordNotes.term: οἶδεν κύριος εὐσεβεῖς ἐκ πειρασμοῦ ῥύεσθαι (oiden kyrios eusebeis ek peirasmou rhyesthai) — the Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations
wordNotes.explanation: Oida with an infinitive expresses knowing how, and therefore being able, to act. Peirasmos includes both trials and enticements. The promise is that the Lord can bring his devout people safely out of the testing they face, as he did Noah and Lot.

wordNotes.term: εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως κολαζομένους τηρεῖν (eis hēmeran kriseōs kolazomenous tērein) — to reserve unto the day of judgment to be punished
wordNotes.explanation: Tēreō again means to keep in custody. The present participle kolazomenous may express the purpose of the keeping, punishment at the judgment, or describe sin’s present consequences while the verdict waits. Either way, the decisive reckoning belongs to the coming day of judgment.

verses.bibleText: But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But chiefly” singles out the class of the unjust Peter has in view: the false teachers themselves. He names two marks that belong together. They “walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness,” going after physical desire wherever it leads. The noun miasmos means defilement or pollution, and it describes desire that stains whoever follows it. And they “despise government,” literally lordship (kyriotēs). Since Peter has already said they deny the Master who bought them (2:1), the lordship they scorn is most likely the authority of Christ himself. Indulgence and contempt for authority are two sides of one rebellion. Those who will not be ruled by Christ end up ruled by their appetites (Romans 8:5–8).

Peter adds a character sketch. “Presumptuous” describes reckless daring, boldness without reverence. “Selfwilled” describes the self-pleasing arrogance that insists on its own way; Paul names it as a disqualification for elders (Titus 1:7). Such people “are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.” The word doxai, “glories,” most naturally refers to angelic beings. Whether Peter means holy angels whom the teachers belittled, or spiritual powers in general whose reality they mocked, the point is the absence of trembling. They speak with careless contempt about the unseen world they claim to have outgrown.

A useful test of any teaching is the reverence it shows toward God and the spiritual realities he has revealed. Teaching that treats holy things lightly will soon treat moral boundaries lightly as well. The fear of the Lord, by contrast, is the beginning of wisdom and the guard of a clean life.

wordNotes.term: κυριότητος καταφρονοῦντας (kyriotētos kataphronountas) — despise government
wordNotes.explanation: Kyriotēs means lordship or dominion. In some passages it refers to angelic ranks, but here, after the denial of the Master in 2:1, it most likely refers to the Lord’s own authority. Kataphroneō means to look down on with contempt.

wordNotes.term: δόξας οὐ τρέμουσιν βλασφημοῦντες (doxas ou tremousin blasphēmountes) — they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “they do not tremble as they blaspheme glories.” Doxai most likely refers to glorious angelic beings. The participle describes reviling speech, and the verb of trembling exposes the teachers’ complete lack of reverence.

verses.bibleText: Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter sets the teachers beside the angels. The angels are “greater in power and might” than any human teacher, yet they “bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord.” The context suggests that “them” refers to the dignities of verse 10. Even the mightiest of God’s servants do not pronounce contemptuous verdicts on other spiritual beings, not even fallen ones. They leave sentencing to God.

Jude supplies an example. When Michael the archangel disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a reviling accusation but said, “The Lord rebuke thee” (Jude 1:9). The same words appear when Satan stands to accuse Joshua the high priest (Zechariah 3:2). The angels serve “before the Lord,” in his very presence, and their nearness to him produces restraint. The teachers, who also live under his eye whether they know it or not, show none.

The contrast is pointed. The strongest exercise the most restraint, and the weakest speak the most recklessly. Confronting evil does not require contempt, and opposing error does not license abusive speech. Believers who answer false teaching, including the teaching described in this chapter, are to speak truth while leaving vengeance and final verdicts with God (Romans 12:19).

wordNotes.term: βλάσφημον κρίσιν (blasphēmon krisin) — railing accusation
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means a reviling or slanderous judgment, a verdict delivered with insult. Holy angels refrain from such speech, entrusting judgment to the Lord, which exposes the irreverence of the teachers who revile freely.

verses.bibleText: But these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not; and shall utterly perish in their own corruption;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter turns the teachers’ claims of enlightenment upside down. They present themselves as people of superior insight, free from old fears. He compares them to “natural brute beasts,” creatures without reason that live by instinct. The phrase “made to be taken and destroyed” draws on the image of animals born only to be hunted and killed. For all their talk of liberty, these men live at the level of appetite, and like animals that follow the scent of bait into a trap, they move toward their own capture without understanding it.

They “speak evil of the things that they understand not.” The reviling of verse 10 now receives its diagnosis: ignorance. They mock spiritual realities they have never grasped, and their ignorance is not innocent. The light was available to them, since they had known the way of righteousness (2:21), and they chose to treat it with contempt.

The final clause contains a wordplay that the KJV smooths into “shall utterly perish in their own corruption.” More literally, “in their destruction they will also be destroyed.” The noun and verb share the root phthora, which covers both moral rot and the decay that ends in death. The corruption they embrace becomes the destruction they receive. Sin carries its own wages (Romans 6:23; Galatians 6:8).

The language is that of ending. The Psalms describe those who will not understand as being “like the beasts that perish” (Psalm 49:20), and the wicked as vanishing like smoke (Psalm 37:20). Jesus spoke of God destroying both soul and body (Matthew 10:28). Peter does not picture the false teachers living on forever in suffering. He pictures them perishing, their existence brought to the end their choices have pursued.

wordNotes.term: ἄλογα ζῷα γεγεννημένα φυσικὰ (aloga zōa gegennēmena physika) — natural brute beasts
wordNotes.explanation: Aloga means without reason, and zōa means living creatures. The participle and adverb describe creatures born to live by mere nature and instinct. Peter uses the image to expose teachers who claim insight but are ruled by appetite.

wordNotes.term: ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ αὐτῶν καὶ φθαρήσονται (en tē phthora autōn kai phtharēsontai) — shall utterly perish in their own corruption
wordNotes.explanation: The noun phthora and the verb phtheirō share a root. Peter plays on the double sense of moral corruption and destruction: those who give themselves to corruption will be destroyed by it. The sentence describes a final end, not an endless condition.

verses.bibleText: And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness” states the principle of just recompense. Many manuscripts read a participle meaning “suffering wrong,” which produces a sharper wordplay: they will be wronged as the wages of their wrongdoing. Either way, the harvest matches the sowing. They seek payment for their teaching (2:3, 15), and they will receive a payment they did not bargain for.

They “count it pleasure to riot in the day time.” The word for riot, tryphē, describes soft, luxurious indulgence, and hēdonē, pleasure, often carries a sensual sense. Even pagan moralists regarded daytime carousing as disgraceful, the mark of people beyond shame (Isaiah 5:11). Paul urged believers to walk honestly “as in the day” (Romans 13:13). These teachers have lost even the instinct to hide.

“Spots they are and blemishes.” The words are the reverse of what Peter says about Christ, the Lamb “without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19), and of what he will urge believers to be when the Lord returns, “without spot, and blameless” (3:14). The teachers stain the very community that is meant to reflect the purity of its Redeemer.

They are “sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you.” Some manuscripts read agapais, “love feasts,” instead of apatais, “deceivings,” and Jude 12 speaks of these men as spots in the church’s love feasts. The two words differ by little in Greek, and Peter may be playing on the likeness. The setting in any case is the fellowship meal, where believers shared food and remembered the Lord. The teachers are still at the table. They are not attacking from outside but reveling inside, turning a meal of love into an occasion for self-indulgence, much as some at Corinth had done (1 Corinthians 11:20–22).

wordNotes.term: σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι (spiloi kai mōmoi) — spots and blemishes
wordNotes.explanation: Spilos is a stain and mōmos a defect or blemish. The pair inverts the language of sacrificial purity applied to Christ and to the church that is to be presented without spot or blemish.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ταῖς ἀπάταις αὐτῶν (en tais apatais autōn) — with their own deceivings
wordNotes.explanation: Apatē means deceit or deceptive pleasure. A strong manuscript tradition reads agapais, “love feasts,” matching Jude 12. Whichever reading is original, the context places the teachers at the church’s fellowship meals, indulging themselves through deception.

verses.bibleText: Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The portrait moves from the table to the heart. They have “eyes full of adultery,” literally full of an adulteress. Their gaze cannot rest on a woman without appraising her as a conquest. Jesus located adultery first in the look of the heart (Matthew 5:28), and these men have made that look a permanent habit. Their eyes also “cannot cease from sin.” The adjective means restless, unable to stop. Appetite fed only grows hungrier, which is why Paul describes those given over to sensuality as working uncleanness “with greediness” (Ephesians 4:19).

They are “beguiling unstable souls.” The verb deleazō comes from fishing and hunting; it means to bait a hook or a trap. The targets are the unstable, those not yet firmly set. Peter has called his readers “established” in the truth (1:12) and will close by warning them not to fall from their own steadfastness (3:17). The same root appears in all three places. Stability in the truth is the defense against bait.

“An heart they have exercised with covetous practices.” The verb is gymnazō, to train as an athlete trains. These men have disciplined themselves, but in the wrong direction. Their greed is a practiced skill. Paul told Timothy to exercise himself unto godliness (1 Timothy 4:7). The same capacity for training can build either character or corruption.

“Cursed children” is a Hebrew way of saying they belong to the curse and stand under it. The only escape from such a curse lies in the One who became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

wordNotes.term: δελεάζοντες ψυχὰς ἀστηρίκτους (deleazontes psychas astēriktous) — beguiling unstable souls
wordNotes.explanation: Deleazō means to lure with bait. Astēriktos means unsupported or not firmly set, from the same root as “established” in 1:12 and “stedfastness” in 3:17. The false teachers prey especially on believers who are not yet grounded.

wordNotes.term: καρδίαν γεγυμνασμένην πλεονεξίας (kardian gegymnasmenēn pleonexias) — an heart they have exercised with covetous practices
wordNotes.explanation: Gymnazō is the vocabulary of athletic training. Elsewhere it describes discipline toward godliness or spiritual discernment; here it describes a heart trained by repeated practice in greed.

verses.bibleText: Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
These teachers “have forsaken the right way.” The phrase implies they were once on it. The “right” or straight way is the road of faithful obedience (Acts 13:10), and leaving it means wandering, which is what “gone astray” describes. The verb planaō pictures a traveler who has lost the road and is drifting wherever the ground leads.

They are “following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor.” Numbers calls him the son of Beor (Numbers 22:5); the form Bosor may reflect a regional pronunciation. Balaam was a seer from Mesopotamia hired by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel. God forbade him, and Balaam knew it, but he kept asking for permission to go because the reward was large (Numbers 22:7, 15–19). Peter identifies the heart of the matter: he “loved the wages of unrighteousness.” The same phrase described the teachers’ recompense in verse 13.

Balaam’s story did not end on the hills overlooking Israel’s camp. When he could not curse the people, he counseled Moab to draw them into sexual immorality and idolatry at Baal-peor, and a plague followed (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14). Greed and seduction into sensuality were his combined legacy, and that is precisely the pattern Peter sees in the false teachers.

Balaam’s case is sobering because he possessed real gifts. He heard from God and spoke true oracles about the coming Star out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17). Gifting is no guarantee of faithfulness. A divided heart can use spiritual capacities for selfish ends, and the love of money is a root that grows every kind of evil (1 Timothy 6:10).

wordNotes.term: καταλείποντες εὐθεῖαν ὁδὸν (kataleipontes eutheian hodon) — which have forsaken the right way
wordNotes.explanation: Euthys means straight or upright, and hodos means way. The participle of kataleipō describes abandoning a path one has been on. Peter presents the teachers as apostates who once walked the straight road.

wordNotes.term: μισθὸν ἀδικίας ἠγάπησεν (misthon adikias ēgapēsen) — loved the wages of unrighteousness
wordNotes.explanation: Misthos is pay or wages; adikia is unrighteousness. Balaam’s desire for Balak’s reward drove his conduct. The phrase connects Balaam’s greed to the teachers who treat ministry as a source of gain.

verses.bibleText: But was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Balaam “was rebuked for his iniquity.” The word for iniquity, paranomia, means law-breaking, acting against what God had said. His wrongdoing did not go unnoticed. The rebuke came from the least likely source: “the dumb ass speaking with man’s voice.” The beast of burden, by nature voiceless, was given words while the prophet, who prided himself on seeing, could not see the angel standing in the road with a drawn sword (Numbers 22:22–31).

The donkey “forbad the madness of the prophet.” Paraphronia means being out of one’s right mind. Greed had unbalanced Balaam’s judgment until he was beating the animal that was saving his life. The Greek sets paranomia beside paraphronia, lawlessness beside madness, as if to say that the one produces the other.

The irony points at the false teachers. They boast of insight yet are less perceptive than Balaam’s donkey, and in verse 12 Peter has already compared them to unreasoning animals. There is also mercy in the story. God stopped Balaam on the road and gave him a warning he could not miss. The teachers have had warnings too, including the letter Peter is writing. The question is whether they will be halted before the road ends.

wordNotes.term: παραφρονίαν (paraphronian) — madness
wordNotes.explanation: The noun describes being beside oneself, out of sound mind. Peter places it close to paranomia, “iniquity,” suggesting that persistent law-breaking leads to a loss of moral sanity. Balaam’s greed made him irrational.

verses.bibleText: These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter leaves Balaam and speaks of the teachers directly through two pictures drawn from the dry lands of the East. “These are wells without water.” A traveler in arid country plans his route around springs. To reach one and find it dry is worse than never having counted on it. The teachers advertise refreshment and deliver nothing. Jeremiah described Israel forsaking the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13); Jesus offered water that becomes a spring of everlasting life within (John 4:14). These teachers offer neither.

They are also “clouds that are carried with a tempest.” The better-attested reading is “mists driven by a squall,” haze that promises rain to a parched field and then blows away (Proverbs 25:14). The image suggests both emptiness and instability. Their message shifts with the winds of desire, and it obscures rather than clarifies.

“To whom the mist of darkness is reserved.” The word for darkness, zophos, is the gloom of verse 4, and “reserved” repeats the keeping language of verses 4 and 9. Those who claimed to bring light are headed for darkness. The words “for ever” are missing from important manuscripts here, though Jude 13 includes them. Where the phrase stands, it marks an outcome that is final and cannot be reversed, the outer darkness of exclusion from God’s presence (Matthew 8:12). It does not describe an unending conscious existence in torment, since Peter has just said such people will utterly perish (2:12).

wordNotes.term: πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι (pēgai anydroi) — wells without water
wordNotes.explanation: Pēgē is a spring or fountain, and anydros means waterless. In a dry climate a waterless spring is a cruel deception. The image captures teaching that promises spiritual refreshment but has no life to give.

wordNotes.term: ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους τετήρηται (ho zophos tou skotous tetērētai) — the mist of darkness is reserved
wordNotes.explanation: Zophos means deep gloom, the same word used in 2:4. The perfect passive verb, “has been kept,” presents the outcome as already settled by God. The phrase describes final exclusion from the light of God’s presence.

verses.bibleText: For when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Peter describes their speech and their targets. They “speak great swelling words of vanity.” The adjective means overswollen or inflated, the bombast of impressive phrases with nothing inside them. “Vanity,” mataiotēs, is emptiness. Their rhetoric is large and hollow at once.

With it they “allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness.” The verb is the baiting word of verse 14 again. The hook is sensuality, the same unrestrained aselgeia of verses 2 and 7. Grand language makes the bait respectable.

The most troubling detail is the identity of their prey: “those that were clean escaped from them who live in error.” The better-attested reading is “those who are barely escaping,” people only just breaking free from their pagan past. “Them who live in error” are their former companions in idolatry and indulgence (1 Peter 4:3–4). New converts, still unsteady, are lured back toward the very life they were leaving. Jesus reserved some of his sternest words for anyone who causes such little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).

The church’s duty follows. New believers need to be grounded, fed with the pure milk of the word (1 Peter 2:2), and surrounded by mature friends, so that inflated words do not toss them about (Ephesians 4:14).

wordNotes.term: ὑπέρογκα ματαιότητος (hyperonka mataiotētos) — great swelling words of vanity
wordNotes.explanation: Hyperonkos means excessive or puffed up, and mataiotēs means futility. The phrase describes pompous speech that sounds weighty but has no substance.

wordNotes.term: τοὺς ὀλίγως ἀποφεύγοντας (tous oligōs apopheugontas) — those that were clean escaped
wordNotes.explanation: The better-attested text reads oligōs, “barely” or “just now,” with a present participle: those who are only beginning to escape. Peter is describing recent converts still emerging from paganism.

verses.bibleText: While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The teachers’ central slogan is freedom: “they promise them liberty.” Freedom was among the most prized values of the Greco-Roman world, celebrated by politicians and philosophers alike. Within the church, the promise may have twisted the apostolic message of grace and liberty in Christ into license, the very abuse Paul had to resist (Galatians 5:13; 2 Peter 3:15–16). It may also have included freedom from fear of judgment, since the teachers denied that Christ would return to judge.

Peter exposes the irony: “they themselves are the servants of corruption.” Those who offer liberty are slaves. The word phthora, corruption, recalls 1:4, where believers have escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust. It means moral decay and also the decay that ends in death. The teachers cannot lift anyone higher than they are themselves, and they are chained.

The proverb that follows comes from the battlefield: “for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.” In the ancient world a defeated soldier could become his conqueror’s slave. Whatever wins the struggle within a person becomes that person’s master. Jesus said the same: whoever commits sin is the servant of sin, and if the Son makes you free, you are free indeed (John 8:34–36). Paul made the point that we are slaves of whatever we obey, whether of sin unto death or of obedience unto righteousness (Romans 6:16).

Freedom in Scripture is never the absence of any master. It is release from the wrong master into the service of the right one. The teachers have denied the Master who bought them (2:1) and have fallen under another. Real liberty is found in belonging to Christ and walking by what James calls the perfect law of liberty (James 1:25), where obedience flows from a heart set free.

wordNotes.term: δοῦλοι τῆς φθορᾶς (douloi tēs phthoras) — the servants of corruption
wordNotes.explanation: Doulos means slave. Phthora joins moral corruption with the decay that leads to death. Those who promise liberty are themselves owned by the corruption they excuse.

wordNotes.term: ἥττηται, τούτῳ δεδούλωται (hēttētai, toutō dedoulōtai) — is overcome, … is he brought in bondage
wordNotes.explanation: Hēttaomai means to be defeated, and douloō means to enslave. The perfect tenses describe a settled condition. The proverb states a moral law: whatever defeats a person rules that person.

verses.bibleText: For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For if” introduces the deepest tragedy in the chapter. Peter describes people who “have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.” Every phrase echoes the experience of real believers. The “knowledge” is epignōsis, the full, personal knowledge of Christ through which grace and peace are multiplied (1:2) and by which the divine power gives everything needed for life and godliness (1:3). The escape is the escape of 1:4. These people had been set free from the defilements of their former life by coming to know Jesus.

Then they are “again entangled therein, and overcome.” The verb emplekō describes being caught up and woven into something, as a soldier can become tangled in civilian affairs (2 Timothy 2:4) or a fighter in a net. They did not stumble once and rise again. They were drawn back and defeated, and verse 19 has told us what defeat means: bondage.

“The latter end is worse with them than the beginning.” The words echo Jesus’ saying about the unclean spirit that returns to a swept house with seven others, so that the last state of the man is worse than the first (Matthew 12:43–45). Knowledge rejected leaves a person harder than before, with a conscience calloused and an excuse ready for every appeal.

Peter treats this as a real possibility, and that is what gives his warnings force. He has urged his readers to make their calling and election sure, so that they will never fall (1:10), and he will close by urging them to beware lest they fall from their own steadfastness (3:17). The warning does not undermine assurance. Assurance rests in the Lord who knows how to keep the godly (2:9), and those who continue to walk with him are kept. The danger lies in leaving his company for the world he rescued them from.

wordNotes.term: τὰ μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου (ta miasmata tou kosmou) — the pollutions of the world
wordNotes.explanation: Miasma means a defilement or stain, related to the “uncleanness” of 2:10. The phrase describes the morally polluting influences of a world organized without God, from which knowing Christ had set these people free.

wordNotes.term: ἐμπλακέντες ἡττῶνται (emplakentes hēttōntai) — they are again entangled therein, and overcome
wordNotes.explanation: Emplekō means to be entangled or interwoven, and hēttaomai means to be defeated. Together they picture someone caught again in the world’s snares and conquered by them, reversing a previous escape.

verses.bibleText: For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter states a hard comparison: “it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them.” He does not mean that ignorance saves. He means that knowledge brings accountability, and that rejecting light received is graver than never having received it. Jesus taught the same principle: the servant who knew his lord’s will and did not do it receives the heavier sentence (Luke 12:47–48), and those who heard his words have no cloak for their sin (John 15:22).

“The way of righteousness” is the third of the chapter’s “way” phrases, after the way of truth (2:2) and the right way (2:15). The gospel is a path on which God’s saving righteousness (1:1) produces righteous living. “To turn” may be read “to turn back,” deliberately reversing direction after walking the road.

What they turn from is “the holy commandment.” The singular with the article gathers the whole moral instruction of the gospel into one: the call to holy living that the apostles taught and that Peter will mention again as “the commandment of us the apostles” (3:2). It is “holy” because it comes from the holy God and expresses his character, just as Paul calls the law holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good (Romans 7:12). Grace has not made that commandment obsolete. The new covenant writes God’s law on the heart (Hebrews 8:10), and the faith that saves is a faith that keeps his commandments.

The commandment was “delivered unto them,” handed on as a sacred trust. To turn from it is to turn from the Lord who gave it and the apostles who faithfully passed it on.

wordNotes.term: τῆς παραδοθείσης αὐτοῖς ἁγίας ἐντολῆς (tēs paradotheisēs autois hagias entolēs) — the holy commandment delivered unto them
wordNotes.explanation: Entolē is a commandment; the singular with the article summarizes the whole body of Christian moral instruction. Paradidōmi means to hand over or pass on, the vocabulary of faithfully transmitted teaching. The commandment is holy because it reflects God’s own character.

wordNotes.term: ἐπεγνωκέναι τὴν ὁδὸν τῆς δικαιοσύνης (epegnōkenai tēn hodon tēs dikaiosynēs) — to have known the way of righteousness
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is related to epignōsis, the full knowledge of Christ in this letter. It implies real acquaintance with the gospel way, which makes turning from it a conscious act and increases accountability.

verses.bibleText: But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter seals the chapter with two blunt proverbs. “The dog is turned to his own vomit again” comes from Proverbs 26:11, where it describes the fool who repeats his folly. “The sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire” is not found in the Old Testament but circulated in ancient wisdom sayings. Both animals were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 23:18), and both were used as images of contempt (Matthew 7:6; Philippians 3:2).

The dog returns to what it once expelled. Sin that had been rejected as repulsive becomes appetizing again. The sow had been washed, cleansed on the outside, and goes back to the mud. The washing may recall the purging from old sins mentioned in 1:9, and perhaps baptism. A cleansing that does not continue into a changed life is quickly undone.

The proverbs show why the return happens. Outward reformation without an inward change of nature cannot hold. Peter has already named the remedy: to become partakers of the divine nature through God’s promises (1:4). God promised through Ezekiel to sprinkle clean water on his people and also to give them a new heart and put his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:25–27).

The chapter therefore ends with a warning, and it leads straight into Peter’s final appeal. Remember the words of the prophets and apostles (3:2), beware of being led away (3:17), and grow in grace and in the knowledge of Christ (3:18).

wordNotes.term: τὸ τῆς ἀληθοῦς παροιμίας (to tēs alēthous paroimias) — according to the true proverb
wordNotes.explanation: Paroimia is a proverb or proverbial saying. Calling it “true” means its picture has proved accurate in these people’s case. The first saying is drawn from Proverbs 26:11; the second was a familiar saying of the time.

wordNotes.term: ὗς λουσαμένη (hys lousamenē) — the sow that was washed
wordNotes.explanation: Louō means to wash or bathe the whole body. The washed pig pictures outward cleansing without inner change. Its return to the mire shows that cleansing must be followed by a renewed nature.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can a teacher sound biblical, attract many followers, and still lead people away from Christ?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: False teaching that denies Christ’s lordship and excuses sin leads to destruction, but the Lord who judged the ancient world also knows how to keep and rescue those who remain faithful to him.
discussionQuestions: What three marks of the false teachers appear in verses 1–3, and why does Peter place their motives beside their doctrine?
Why does Peter pair each example of judgment with an example of rescue in verses 4–9?
How does the story of Balaam help explain the danger of religious gifts joined to a divided heart?
In what ways can a promise of freedom become a new form of slavery?
Why is turning back from known truth more serious than never having known it?
commonMisunderstandings: Verses 4 and 9 do not teach that the wicked dead or the fallen angels are now enduring their final punishment; they are kept for a judgment still to come.
The “ashes” of Sodom describe complete destruction, not a fire that continues burning.
Peter’s warning is aimed at those who deny Christ and excuse immorality, not at sincere believers who differ on secondary questions.
The warning about apostasy is not meant to destroy assurance; it calls believers to keep walking with the Lord who keeps them.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the severity of the warning and the strength of the promise: God’s judgment on deliberate rebellion is certain, and his care for the godly who live among corruption is just as certain.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Stay on the straight way with the Master who bought you, test every promise of freedom by his word, and trust him to keep you until the day he comes.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Christ has paid the price for every person, and true freedom is found only by belonging to him; rejecting him leaves a person enslaved to corruption and facing certain judgment.
flow: Every person is mastered by something; whatever overcomes us enslaves us.
Jesus, the true Master, bought us with his own life to set us free from sin.
God has shown in history that he judges persistent rebellion and rescues those who trust him.
Denying the Master does not bring freedom; it leaves a person bound to corruption and its end.
Accepting Christ’s ownership brings cleansing, a new nature, and safe keeping until the day of judgment.
simpleIllustrations: A dry well marked on a desert map is worse than no well at all, because travelers stake their lives on it; empty spiritual promises do the same.
A freed slave who walks back to the auction block has not gained liberty; he has chosen a harder master.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you acknowledge Jesus as the Master who bought you and let him set you free from what has overcome you?
cautions: Do not use this chapter to label every opponent a false teacher; Peter’s criteria are denial of Christ and the excusing of sin.
Do not present God’s judgment without the rescue of Noah and Lot that Peter places beside it.
Avoid describing the fate of the lost as endless conscious burning; Peter speaks of ashes, perishing, and destruction.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I most vulnerable to teaching that flatters my desires instead of shaping them by Christ?
Do I live with Lot’s grief over evil, or have I grown comfortable with what once troubled my conscience?
What would it look like for me to treat Jesus as the Master who bought me, in my money, my body, and my speech?
Which promise of freedom in my culture has proved to be a form of bondage in my own life?
How can I help newer believers become established so that smooth words do not lure them away?
